A retraction is the official act of taking back something that was previously said, written, published, or claimed — because it was wrong, false, misleading, or should not have been stated in the first place.

Think of it like this: you shot an arrow. A retraction is you pulling that arrow back and saying, "That arrow should never have been fired."

It's not just admitting a mistake. It is the formal, public act of cancelling or withdrawing the original statement so that it no longer stands.
The Two Core Elements of Every Retraction

Every retraction has two parts working together:

  1. A withdrawal — "What I said/published/claimed is no longer valid. Take it back."
  2. An implicit or explicit acknowledgment — "It was wrong, false, or made in error."

Without both of these, it's not truly a retraction. It might just be an update, a correction, or an apology.

1. In Journalism and Media

This is the most common place you'll see the word. When a newspaper, magazine, or news website publishes a story that turns out to be false or factually wrong, they publish a retraction — a formal statement that says: "We reported X. That was incorrect. We are withdrawing that report."

"The newspaper issued a retraction after it was discovered that the story about the politician was based on fabricated evidence."

A retraction in journalism is considered a serious, significant event. It signals that the original report caused real harm or damage to someone's reputation, and the publisher is taking full responsibility by officially pulling it back.

2. In Science and Academic Research

When a scientist publishes a research paper and it is later found to contain errors, manipulated data, or even outright fraud, the journal publishes a retraction of that paper.

"The medical journal published a retraction of the study after peer reviewers found that the data had been falsified."

A retraction in science is a very serious matter. It means the research should not be used, cited, or trusted anymore. It is essentially erasing the paper from the record of accepted knowledge — not correcting it, but withdrawing it entirely.

3. In Law and Legal Proceedings

In legal contexts, a retraction means formally taking back an accusation, statement, or claim that was made — especially if it was false or defamatory.

"The defendant demanded a retraction of the false accusations made against him in public."

Here, a retraction can sometimes protect someone from a lawsuit, because it shows the person acknowledged their statement was wrong and withdrew it.

4. In Everyday Life and Conversation

You can also use "retraction" in ordinary situations, though it sounds more formal than casual speech. It simply means someone is taking back what they said.

"After the heated argument, she issued a retraction of her harsh words."
What Makes a Retraction Different from Similar Words?

This is important for truly understanding the word.

Retraction vs. Correction
A correction fixes the wrong information and replaces it with the right information. The original piece still exists, just with an amendment. A retraction removes or cancels the original claim entirely — it doesn't replace it with correct information; it says the whole thing should not have been said.

A correction says: "We said the event happened on Monday. It actually happened on Tuesday."
A retraction says: "We reported that the event happened. It never happened at all. We withdraw that report."

Retraction vs. Apology
An apology expresses regret. A retraction takes action. You can apologize without retracting, and you can retract without apologizing. But a retraction has practical, real-world consequences — the original claim is officially nullified. An apology alone doesn't achieve that.

Retraction vs. Denial
A denial says something didn't happen ("I never said that"). A retraction acknowledges that something was indeed said or published — and now it's being pulled back. Denials look forward; retractions look back at something that actually occurred and undo it.
The Weight and Tone of the Word

"Retraction" is a formal, serious word. When you use it, it signals:

  • Something was officially stated in a public or professional setting.
  • That statement has been officially withdrawn.
  • There is an acknowledgment that it was wrong or harmful.

It carries a sense of accountability. A retraction is not something done quietly. It is usually made in the same public space where the original statement appeared — if something was printed in a newspaper, the retraction is also printed in that newspaper. The purpose is to undo the damage to the audience and to the person who was harmed by the original statement.

• "The magazine's retraction came too late — the false story had already spread across the internet."
  • "He demanded a public retraction from the journalist who had defamed him."
  • "The retraction of the drug study threw years of medical research into doubt."
  • "Her retraction of the accusation helped restore his damaged reputation."
  • "Despite the retraction, many people still believed the original story."

A retraction is a formal, public withdrawal of something previously said, published, or claimed — an official statement that says: "That should not have been put out there, and we are taking it back."
